title: Classifying a browser-based CRM subscription
question: A sales team subscribes to a hosted CRM product. They use it in the browser, configure users and fields, and the vendor runs the servers, the application and its upgrades. Which service model is this?
options: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
Platform as a Service (PaaS)
Software as a Service (SaaS)
Function as a Service (FaaS)
explanation: In SaaS the provider delivers and operates a complete application; the customer only configures and uses it. PaaS would still require the team to deploy its own code, IaaS would require managing VMs and operating systems, and FaaS is a way to run your own functions, not a finished product.

title: Workload that needs a kernel driver on the host OS
question: A vendor's licensing agent must be installed as a kernel driver plus a Windows service with administrator rights on the operating system that runs the application. Which service model can host this workload?
options: A PaaS web hosting service with a custom startup script
IaaS virtual machines where the team controls the guest OS
A serverless function platform with a larger memory setting
A SaaS product that offers an equivalent built-in feature
explanation: Only IaaS gives you administrative control of the operating system, so you can install drivers and system services. PaaS and serverless platforms manage the OS for you and run your code in a sandbox without kernel-level access, and switching to a SaaS product does not host the vendor's agent at all.

title: What you still own after moving to a managed database
question: A team moves from SQL Server on VMs to a managed PaaS database (Azure SQL Database). Which task is still the team's responsibility after the move?
options: Applying operating system and database engine patches
Configuring automated backups and the storage they use
Designing indexes and tuning the queries the app sends
Replacing failed disks and hardware in the data center
explanation: A managed database service takes over patching, automated backups, high availability and hardware, but the schema, indexes, query design and data access control remain the customer's job. A slow query caused by a missing index is still your problem on PaaS, even though the platform may offer tuning recommendations.

title: Who is accountable for an over-shared SaaS document
question: In a SaaS file-sharing product, an employee shared a folder of customer contracts with 'anyone with the link', and it leaked. The vendor's platform worked as designed. Under the shared responsibility model, who owned this risk?
options: The SaaS vendor, because in SaaS the provider owns all security layers
The cloud provider hosting the vendor, as it controls the physical hosts
Nobody, since sharing links are a product feature outside the model
The customer, since data, accounts and access settings remain theirs
explanation: Even in SaaS, the customer always keeps responsibility for its data, identities and how access is configured. The vendor secures the application and infrastructure, but it cannot decide which documents your users should share; sharing policies, DLP and user training are the customer's controls.

title: Containers versus virtual machines
question: Which statement best describes a key difference between containers and virtual machines?
options: Containers share the host's OS kernel; each VM runs its own guest OS
Containers need a hypervisor per app; VMs run directly on the kernel
Containers always persist their state; VMs are always ephemeral
Containers can only run on Linux; VMs can only run on Windows hosts
explanation: Containers isolate processes using kernel features such as namespaces and cgroups while sharing the host kernel, which makes them lighter and faster to start. A VM virtualizes hardware through a hypervisor and boots a full guest operating system. Container filesystems are ephemeral by default, and both technologies run on Linux and Windows.

title: A batch Lambda starving latency-critical functions
question: A bulk import fans out thousands of invocations of an import Lambda function. During each import, the latency-critical API functions in the same account and region start failing with throttling errors. What is the most direct fix?
options: Raise the import function's memory so each invocation ends sooner
Configure reserved concurrency to cap the import function's share
Move the API functions to a different VPC in the same account
Increase the timeout of the API functions so they wait for capacity
explanation: Lambda concurrency is a pool shared by all functions in an account and region, so a burst from one function can consume it and throttle the others. Reserved concurrency both guarantees and limits a function's concurrency, so capping the import function (or reserving capacity for the API) isolates them. VPC placement and timeouts do not change the shared limit, and more memory only shortens, not caps, the burst.

title: Shared filesystem for several Linux VMs
question: Ten Linux VMs must mount the same directory at the same time and read and write files with normal POSIX file semantics. Which storage type fits?
options: A managed network file system such as Amazon EFS
An object storage bucket accessed through its REST API
A block storage volume attached to one of the VMs
A key-value database table holding file contents
explanation: A managed file service (for example Amazon EFS over NFS, or Azure Files) exposes a shared filesystem that many instances can mount concurrently. Block volumes are normally attached to a single instance, and object storage and key-value databases are accessed through APIs rather than as a mounted POSIX filesystem.

title: Stale reads after adding a read replica
question: To offload the primary database, all SELECT queries now go to an asynchronous read replica. Users report that right after saving their profile, the page sometimes shows the old values. What is happening and what is a common fix?
options: The replica cache must be flushed after every write from the app
Replication lag; read a user's own recent writes from the primary
The primary loses commits; switch it to a larger instance class
The ORM batches writes; disable batching so saves are synchronous
explanation: Read replicas apply changes asynchronously, so a read issued just after a write may hit a replica that has not caught up yet. Routing read-your-own-writes paths (or reads shortly after a write) to the primary restores the expected behavior. The primary has not lost data, and there is no replica cache to flush.

title: Preventing two writers from creating the same S3 key
question: Several workers may try to create the same S3 object key at the same time, and only the first one must succeed, without adding a separate lock service. What does S3 offer for this?
options: Enable bucket versioning so a second PUT is rejected automatically
Use S3 Object Lock in governance mode on the key before writing
Read the key first and only PUT when a HEAD request returns 404
A conditional PUT with If-None-Match: * so later writers get 412
explanation: S3 supports conditional writes: a PutObject with If-None-Match: * succeeds only if no object exists at that key, and concurrent losers receive 412 Precondition Failed. A HEAD-then-PUT check is racy, versioning simply keeps both versions, and Object Lock protects existing versions from deletion rather than arbitrating creation.

title: Usable addresses in a small AWS subnet
question: You create an AWS VPC subnet with a /28 IPv4 CIDR block. How many IP addresses can you assign to resources in it?
options: 16, because a /28 block contains 16 addresses
14, because only network and broadcast are reserved
11, because AWS reserves 5 addresses per subnet
8, because half of the block is kept for failover
explanation: A /28 has 2^(32-28) = 16 addresses, and AWS reserves the first four and the last one in every subnet (network, VPC router, DNS, future use, broadcast), leaving 11. Traditional on-premises math reserves only 2 addresses, which is why teams often under-size cloud subnets.

title: Health checks that take down a healthy fleet
question: The load balancer health check calls /health, which runs a query against the shared database. During a short database slowdown, every instance failed its check, autoscaling replaced them all, and the outage got much worse. What change addresses the root cause?
options: Use a shallow liveness check for replacement, and handle dependency health separately
Lower the health-check interval so failing instances are replaced more quickly
Add more database read replicas so the health query never becomes slow
Remove health checks entirely and rely on users to report broken instances
explanation: A deep check that depends on a shared dependency makes all instances fail together, so the load balancer and autoscaler remove healthy capacity during a dependency problem. Checks used to replace or route around hosts should test local health; dependency problems should be surfaced through metrics or degraded-mode handling. Faster replacement amplifies the cascade, and removing checks loses detection of real host failures.

title: Applying least privilege to a CI job
question: A new CI job only needs to upload build artifacts to one prefix of one S3 bucket. Which permission grant follows the principle of least privilege?
options: The AdministratorAccess managed policy, scoped later
s3:* on all buckets so future jobs can reuse the role
s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::builds/artifacts/* only
Read and write access to every object in the bucket
explanation: Least privilege means granting only the actions and resources a principal needs: here, PutObject on the specific prefix. Broad grants such as s3:* or AdministratorAccess enlarge the blast radius if the CI credentials leak, and 'scope it later' rarely happens in practice.

title: Responding to a secret pushed to a public repository
question: A developer pushed a cloud API key to a public Git repository, noticed it ten minutes later, and rewrote history with a force-push to remove it. What is the most important next step?
options: Nothing more; the commit no longer appears on the default branch
Make the repository private so the old commit becomes unreachable
Revoke and rotate the key, then review logs for any use while exposed
Ask the hosting provider to purge cached views of the old commit
explanation: Once a secret has been public, assume it is compromised: automated scanners harvest keys within minutes, and clones, forks or caches may keep the old commit. Rewriting history or changing visibility does not invalidate the credential, so revoke and rotate it first and check audit logs for misuse. Purging caches is optional cleanup, not mitigation.

title: Protecting a role assumed by a third-party SaaS
question: A third-party monitoring SaaS assumes an IAM role in your account using its own AWS account as the principal. What prevents another customer of that SaaS from configuring your role ARN and tricking the vendor into accessing your account?
options: Requiring MFA in the trust policy for the vendor's AWS account
A unique sts:ExternalId condition in the role's trust policy
Attaching a permissions boundary to the vendor-assumed role
Rotating the role's access keys every 90 days via automation
explanation: This is the confused deputy problem: the vendor is trusted, but could be induced to act for the wrong customer. Requiring a secret, customer-specific ExternalId in the trust policy means the vendor can only assume the role when acting for you. Roles have no long-term access keys, MFA cannot be supplied by an automated service, and a boundary limits permissions but not who can trigger their use.

title: Backups that have never been restored
question: A team copies nightly database backups to a second region and claims an RTO of 2 hours, but no one has ever performed a restore. What is the most valuable next step for the DR plan?
options: Increase backup frequency to hourly so the RPO also improves
Encrypt the backup copies with a separate customer-managed key
Regularly run restore and failover drills and time them against the RTO
Replicate the backups to a third region for additional redundancy
explanation: An untested backup is an assumption, not a recovery capability: restores fail due to missing permissions, dependencies, runbook gaps or durations far longer than expected. Regular drills validate that recovery works and that the measured time meets the RTO. More copies, more frequent backups or extra encryption do not prove that recovery is possible.

title: Telemetry that shows a request's path across services
question: A checkout request passes through an API gateway, three microservices and a database, and you need to see where its 3 seconds were spent. Which telemetry signal is designed for this?
options: Aggregated metrics such as average CPU per service
Distributed traces made of spans for each operation
Unstructured log lines written by each service host
Infrastructure inventory and configuration snapshots
explanation: A distributed trace links spans across services through a shared trace ID, with timing for each step, so you can see which hop consumed the latency. Metrics are aggregated and lose per-request detail, and logs without correlation IDs cannot easily be stitched into one request path.

title: Average latency hides a slow tail
question: A dashboard shows average API latency of 120 ms, well within target, yet many users complain about very slow pages. Which change to the monitoring is most likely to reveal the problem?
options: Track latency percentiles such as p95 and p99 per endpoint
Lengthen the averaging window from 1 minute to 1 hour
Add more CPU and memory metrics for every application host
Replace latency monitoring with a request-count throughput alert
explanation: Latency distributions are usually long-tailed, so an average can look fine while a meaningful fraction of requests is very slow. Percentiles such as p95 and p99 expose that tail, which is what users actually experience on slow pages. A longer averaging window hides the problem even more, and resource or throughput metrics do not measure user latency.

title: Error budget for a 99.9% monthly SLO
question: A service has an availability SLO of 99.9% measured over a 30-day window. Roughly how much full downtime does its error budget allow in that window?
options: About 4 minutes
About 43 minutes
About 7 hours
About 3 days
explanation: The error budget is 100% minus the SLO, here 0.1%. Thirty days contain 43,200 minutes, and 0.1% of that is about 43.2 minutes. About 4 minutes corresponds to a 99.99% SLO, about 7 hours to 99%, and several days of downtime to an SLO near 90%.

title: A user_id label that overwhelms Prometheus
question: A developer added a user_id label to the http_requests_total counter so that per-user traffic could be graphed. Within days the Prometheus server's memory use and query times exploded. Why?
options: Counters reset on restart, so per-user counters are stored twice
Prometheus must scrape each user label from a separate target
Labels are stored as strings inside each sample's float value
Every distinct label value creates a new time series to store
explanation: In Prometheus each unique combination of label values is a separate time series, so an unbounded label like user_id multiplies the series count by the number of users. Prometheus guidance warns against labels with high cardinality such as user IDs or email addresses; that kind of per-entity analysis belongs in logs, traces or an analytics store.

title: Restoring an object deleted from a versioned bucket
question: In an S3 bucket with versioning enabled, someone ran a simple DELETE on report.csv (no version ID), and GET now returns 404. How do you bring the object back?
options: Restore it from the S3 Glacier tier, where deleted objects are moved
Ask AWS Support to recover it, since deletes are not reversible
Delete the delete marker so the prior version becomes current again
Turn versioning off and back on to reapply the latest object version
explanation: With versioning enabled, a simple DELETE does not remove data; it inserts a delete marker as the current version, so GET returns 404. Permanently deleting that marker (by its version ID) makes the previous version current again. Objects are not moved to Glacier on delete, and versioning cannot be turned off once enabled, only suspended.

title: Google Cloud's serverless analytics warehouse
question: Analysts want to run SQL over terabytes of data in Google Cloud without provisioning or managing any database servers or clusters. Which service is designed for this?
options: BigQuery
Cloud SQL
Bigtable
Firestore
explanation: BigQuery is a fully managed, serverless data warehouse for analytical SQL at very large scale. Cloud SQL is a managed transactional database (MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server) with sized instances, Bigtable is a wide-column NoSQL store for low-latency key access, and Firestore is a document database for applications.

title: Connecting VMs in two regions on Google Cloud
question: A team used to AWS plans to create one VPC in us-central1 and another in europe-west1, then peer them, so VMs in both regions can talk over private IPs. What is true in Google Cloud?
options: Peering is required, because Google Cloud VPCs are always regional
A Cloud VPN tunnel is needed for any traffic between two regions
Private IPs only work inside one zone, so external IPs are needed
One VPC is enough: VPCs are global and their subnets are regional
explanation: A Google Cloud VPC network is a global resource, while its subnets are regional. VMs in subnets of the same VPC can communicate over internal IPs across regions without peering or VPN. That differs from AWS, where a VPC lives in one region.

title: Serverless Functions plan with VNet access and warm instances
question: An event-driven Functions app must reach a database through a private endpoint in a VNet, should avoid cold starts on its HTTP trigger, and should still scale out on demand with serverless billing. Which hosting option fits best?
options: The Flex Consumption plan with VNet integration and always-ready instances
The legacy Consumption plan with a longer functionTimeout in host.json
A Basic App Service plan with ARR affinity enabled for the Functions app
Durable Functions on the Consumption plan, using an eternal orchestration
explanation: The Flex Consumption plan supports virtual network integration and lets you configure always-ready instances to reduce cold starts while still scaling dynamically with consumption-based billing. The legacy Consumption plan does not support VNet integration, and a longer timeout does not affect cold starts. ARR affinity is about session stickiness, and an eternal orchestration does not keep an HTTP trigger warm.

title: Cheapest blob tier that is still online
question: Compliance backups are kept for at least 180 days and read only a few times a year, but when needed they must be readable immediately, without a rehydration step. Which blob access tier is the cheapest that meets this?
options: Hot tier
Cool tier
Cold tier
Archive tier
explanation: The Cold tier is an online tier with lower storage cost than Cool, intended for data kept at least 90 days and rarely accessed, and it can be read immediately. Archive is cheaper but offline, so blobs must be rehydrated for hours before reading. Hot and Cool are online but cost more to store data that is accessed this rarely.

title: Recovering from an accidental DELETE in Azure SQL Database
question: Two hours ago a script deleted thousands of rows from a table in an Azure SQL Database; other tables kept receiving valid writes since then. How does point-in-time restore help here?
options: It rewinds the existing database in place, discarding all later writes
It restores only the affected table into the live database directly
It requires a geo-replica, since PITR uses the secondary as its source
It creates a new database as of the chosen time; copy the rows back
explanation: Point-in-time restore in Azure SQL Database always creates a new database from the automated backups at the chosen time; it cannot overwrite the existing database or restore a single table in place. You then copy the deleted rows from the restored database into production, preserving the valid writes made since. It works from automated backups and does not need geo-replication.

title: Recovering an accidentally deleted Key Vault secret
question: An engineer accidentally deleted a secret from Azure Key Vault yesterday. How can it be recovered?
options: It cannot be recovered; deletion in Key Vault is always permanent
Recover it from the soft-deleted state within the retention period
Restore the whole vault from the nightly Azure Backup snapshot
Open a support ticket so Microsoft can replay the vault audit log
explanation: Soft delete is enabled on Key Vault and keeps deleted vaults and objects in a recoverable state for a configurable retention period (7 to 90 days). During that time you can recover the secret, unless someone purges it; purge protection can prevent even that. Key Vault is not backed up by Azure Backup snapshots, and audit logs do not contain secret values.

title: Key Vault 429 errors under load
question: An API calls Key Vault GetSecret on every incoming request to read a database password. Under peak load it starts receiving HTTP 429 responses from Key Vault and requests fail. What is the recommended fix?
options: Create several vaults and pick one at random for each request
Switch the vault from the RBAC model to vault access policies
Disable the vault firewall so calls skip network rule evaluation
Cache the secret in memory and refresh it periodically or on failure
explanation: Key Vault enforces service limits per vault, and it is not meant to be called on every request. Microsoft's throttling guidance is to cache secrets in the application, refresh them on an interval or on authentication failure, and use exponential backoff on 429s. Spreading load across vaults adds complexity without fixing the pattern, and the permission model and firewall do not affect throttling.

title: Giving each consumer service its own copy of a message
question: Billing, shipping and analytics services must each receive their own copy of every OrderPlaced message and process it independently. Which Service Bus construct fits?
options: A topic with one subscription for each of the three services
A single queue that all three services read from with competing consumers
Three queues, with the producer choosing one at random per message
One session-enabled queue with a separate session for each service
explanation: A Service Bus topic delivers a copy of each message to every subscription, and each subscription behaves like its own queue for its consumer. With a single queue, consumers compete and each message is processed by only one of them, and random routing or sessions would also give each message to only one service.

title: Filtering traffic to a subnet by port and source
question: You need to allow inbound TCP 443 to a subnet's VMs only from a specific IP range and deny other inbound traffic. Which Azure resource provides these allow/deny rules?
options: A network security group associated with the subnet or NICs
A route table with a user-defined route for that IP range
An Azure DNS private zone linked to the virtual network
A NAT gateway attached to the subnet for its outbound traffic
explanation: Network security groups contain prioritized allow/deny rules based on source, destination, port and protocol, and can be associated with subnets or network interfaces. Route tables control where traffic is sent, not whether it is allowed, a private DNS zone only resolves names, and a NAT gateway provides outbound connectivity.

title: Spoke VNets that cannot reach each other
question: VNet A is peered with hub VNet B, and B is peered with VNet C. VMs in A can reach B, and C can reach B, but A cannot reach C. Why?
options: Peering requires all three VNets to share one address space
Peered VNets must be in the same region to forward traffic
NSGs block all traffic that arrives over any peering link
VNet peering is non-transitive, so A and C are not connected
explanation: VNet peering is not transitive: A-B and B-C peerings do not create an A-C path. You either peer A and C directly, or route spoke-to-spoke traffic through a network virtual appliance or Azure Firewall in the hub (or use Virtual WAN). Peered VNets must have non-overlapping address spaces, global peering works across regions, and default NSG rules allow VNet traffic.

title: App Service that cannot call a private API
question: An App Service app must call an internal API on a VM in a VNet using its private IP. The team created a private endpoint for the App Service app, yet the outbound calls still time out. What is missing?
options: A public IP on the VM so the app can reach it over the internet
Regional VNet integration on the app, since private endpoints are inbound only
A service endpoint for Microsoft.Web on the VM's subnet in the VNet
An access restriction rule on the app that allows the VM's private IP
explanation: A private endpoint gives clients in the VNet a private inbound path to the app; it does nothing for traffic the app sends. Outbound calls from App Service into a VNet require virtual network integration. Access restrictions also only filter inbound traffic, a service endpoint on the VM subnet does not route the app's traffic, and a public IP defeats the purpose.

title: Getting Key Vault audit logs into Log Analytics
question: Security wants to query Key Vault access events (who read which secret) in a Log Analytics workspace, but no such logs appear there. What must be configured?
options: An Application Insights SDK inside the Key Vault resource
A metric alert rule on the vault's ServiceApiHit metric
A diagnostic setting on the vault that sends logs to the workspace
A private endpoint so the vault can reach the workspace
explanation: Resource logs such as Key Vault AuditEvent are not collected by default; you create a diagnostic setting that routes the chosen log categories to a Log Analytics workspace, storage account or event hub. Metrics alerts only evaluate metrics, Application Insights instruments your applications, not Azure resources, and a private endpoint is unrelated to log routing.

title: Detecting an unreachable site with no traffic
question: A public status page gets almost no traffic at night, so request-based alerts never fire when it goes down. You want an alert if it becomes unreachable from several geographic locations. What should you use?
options: A log alert that counts failed requests in the requests table
Smart detection of failure anomalies in Application Insights
Live Metrics in Application Insights watched by the on-call engineer
Application Insights availability tests run from multiple regions
explanation: Availability tests are synthetic probes that send requests to your endpoint from several Azure locations on a schedule and can alert when a number of locations fail, regardless of real user traffic. Request-based log alerts and failure anomaly detection depend on actual traffic, and Live Metrics is a real-time view, not an alerting mechanism.

title: Cutting cost of high-volume, rarely queried logs
question: An app sends about 2 TB per day of verbose debug logs into a Log Analytics custom table. They are queried only occasionally during incident investigations and never used for alerts. Which change cuts ingestion cost most while keeping the data queryable?
options: Set the table to a lower-cost plan such as Basic, paying per query
Increase the workspace's interactive retention to two full years
Enable adaptive sampling in the Application Insights SDK for logs
Move the table to a dedicated cluster without a commitment tier
explanation: Log Analytics tables can use the Analytics, Basic or Auxiliary plan. Basic and Auxiliary have much lower ingestion prices and charge per query, with reduced features, which suits high-volume troubleshooting data that is not used for alerting. Longer retention adds cost, a dedicated cluster requires a commitment tier, and adaptive sampling applies to Application Insights telemetry rather than arbitrary custom tables.

title: Why prefer incremental loads for a huge table
question: A 2 TB source table changes by about 0.1% per day, and a nightly pipeline currently reloads the whole table. What is the main benefit of switching to an incremental load?
options: It guarantees the target will never contain duplicate rows
It copies only new or changed data, cutting time, cost and source load
It removes the need to track any watermark or change information
It makes the pipeline exactly-once even when a run is retried
explanation: An incremental (delta) load moves only rows that changed since the last run, using a watermark column, change tracking or CDC, so it is far faster and cheaper and puts less load on the source. It does require tracking change state, and by itself it does not make reruns idempotent or remove duplicates; the load step still needs merge or overwrite logic for that.

title: A few malformed rows failing a large copy
question: A nightly Azure Data Factory copy of 50 million rows fails entirely because a handful of rows have values incompatible with the sink schema. The business wants the good rows loaded and the bad ones kept for review. What fits?
options: Change every sink column to a string type so no row can ever fail
Retry the copy activity several times until the bad rows succeed
Split the copy into many small copies so failures affect fewer rows
Enable fault tolerance to skip incompatible rows and log them to storage
explanation: The copy activity's fault tolerance settings can skip incompatible rows and write them to a log in storage, so the valid rows load and the rejected ones can be inspected and replayed. Retrying does not change bad data, splitting the copy still fails partitions, and turning every column into a string pushes the problem downstream and loses type safety.

title: Slow single-threaded Spark JDBC extraction
question: A Spark job reads a 500-million-row table with spark.read.jdbc(url, "orders", props). It takes hours, and the Spark UI shows a single task doing all the work. Which change parallelizes the read?
options: Set partitionColumn, lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions
Raise spark.sql.shuffle.partitions so the read uses more tasks
Call repartition(64) on the DataFrame immediately after the read
Increase the fetchsize option so each round trip returns more rows
explanation: Without partitioning options, the JDBC source issues one query from one task. With partitionColumn (numeric, date or timestamp), lowerBound, upperBound and numPartitions, Spark issues parallel range queries. Repartitioning happens after the slow single read, shuffle partitions only affect shuffles, and fetchsize can help throughput but keeps a single connection.

title: Grouping clicks into visits
question: A streaming job must group each user's click events into visits, where a visit ends after 30 minutes without activity. Visits vary from seconds to hours. Which window type fits?
options: Tumbling windows of 30 minutes keyed by user
Sliding windows of 30 minutes with a 1-minute slide
Global windows with a count trigger of 30 events
Session windows with a 30-minute inactivity gap
explanation: Session windows have no fixed length: a window for a key stays open while events keep arriving and closes after a gap of inactivity, which matches the visit definition. Tumbling and sliding windows have fixed boundaries that would split long visits and merge unrelated activity, and a count trigger ignores time gaps entirely.

title: What an Airflow DAG represents
question: In Apache Airflow, what is a DAG?
options: A worker process that executes queued tasks on a schedule
A database table that stores the results returned by tasks
A plugin that connects Airflow to an external system
A collection of tasks with dependencies and no cycles
explanation: A DAG (directed acyclic graph) defines tasks and the dependencies between them, plus scheduling information; acyclic means a task can never depend on itself directly or indirectly. Workers execute task instances, XCom and the metadata database store state and small results, and connections or providers integrate with external systems.

title: Capping concurrent calls to a fragile API across DAGs
question: Forty different Airflow DAGs each have tasks that call a partner API, which fails if more than 5 requests run at once. You need a global cap of 5 concurrent tasks across all of these DAGs. What should you use?
options: Set max_active_runs=5 on every DAG that calls the API
Create a pool with 5 slots and assign those tasks to it
Lower the scheduler's parallelism setting to 5 for the whole cluster
Add retries with exponential backoff to each task calling the API
explanation: Airflow pools limit how many task instances assigned to them can run concurrently, across all DAGs, so a 5-slot pool enforces the global cap. max_active_runs limits runs per DAG, not across DAGs, global parallelism would throttle every unrelated task, and retries react to failures instead of preventing overload.

title: Waiting sensors exhausting worker slots
question: Hundreds of sensors wait up to 6 hours for partner files to land. In the default poke mode they occupy worker slots the whole time, and real processing tasks queue for hours. What is the most efficient fix?
options: Use deferrable operators or sensors that hand waiting to the triggerer
Raise poke_interval on every sensor to one hour to reduce the polling
Replace the sensors with a single PythonOperator that loops with sleep
Increase the number of workers so the sensors have dedicated capacity
explanation: Deferrable operators suspend themselves and hand the wait to a trigger running in the lightweight triggerer process, releasing the worker slot until the condition is met. A longer poke interval in poke mode still holds the slot, a sleeping PythonOperator holds it too, and adding workers only buys more slots to waste.

title: Where sales amounts live in a star schema
question: In a star schema for sales analytics, which table stores one row per sales line with numeric measures such as quantity and amount?
options: The fact table, linked to dimensions by foreign keys
The customer dimension, keyed by a surrogate key
The date dimension, with one row for each calendar day
A bridge table holding the many-to-many relationships
explanation: Fact tables store measurable events at a defined grain (here one row per sales line) with numeric measures and foreign keys to dimensions. Dimension tables such as customer or date hold descriptive attributes used to filter and group facts, and bridge tables resolve many-to-many relationships between them.

title: Reproducing a report from last week's table state
question: Finance needs to rerun last Tuesday's report exactly as it was, but the Delta Lake table has been updated and merged daily since then. What is the most direct way to query the old state?
options: Restore yesterday's storage account snapshot into a new container
Query the table with TIMESTAMP AS OF (or VERSION AS OF) that date
Filter the current table on a load_date column for that Tuesday
Read the raw Parquet files of that date directly, skipping the log
explanation: Delta Lake keeps a transaction log of table versions, so time travel with TIMESTAMP AS OF or VERSION AS OF returns the table exactly as it was, as long as the older data files have not yet been removed by VACUUM. Filtering on a load date misses later updates and deletes, and reading Parquet files without the log can include files that were not part of that version.

title: VACUUM with zero retention breaks readers
question: To save storage, an engineer disabled the retention duration check and ran VACUUM events RETAIN 0 HOURS. Right afterwards a long-running query failed with file-not-found errors, and time travel to yesterday's version stopped working. Why?
options: VACUUM rewrote the transaction log, so all versions now have new IDs
VACUUM compacted small files, which invalidated cached query plans
VACUUM deleted files no longer in the latest version but still in use
VACUUM dropped table statistics, so readers looked for missing files
explanation: VACUUM permanently deletes data files that are not referenced by the current table version and are older than the retention threshold. With zero retention it removed files still needed by in-flight readers and by older versions, which breaks both. That is why Delta enforces a default 7-day threshold and the safety check; VACUUM does not compact files or rewrite the log.

title: Row-oriented format for record-at-a-time streams
question: Events are written one record at a time to Kafka and must carry a compact binary encoding with a schema that supports evolution. Which format is row-oriented and commonly used for this?
options: Parquet
ORC
Avro
CSV
explanation: Avro is a row-oriented binary format with schemas defined in JSON, and it supports schema evolution, which makes it a common choice for streaming records through Kafka with a schema registry. Parquet and ORC are columnar formats optimized for analytical scans of large batches, and CSV has no schema or compact encoding.

title: Making Parquet min/max statistics useful
question: Queries filter on customer_id = ?, but each Parquet file has rows for customer IDs spread across the whole range, so every row group must be read. Which change lets readers skip most row groups?
options: Switch the compression codec from Snappy to Gzip in every file
Partition the table by customer_id into one folder per customer
Convert the customer_id column from an integer to a string type
Sort or cluster data by customer_id before writing the files
explanation: Parquet stores min/max statistics per column chunk, and readers skip row groups whose range cannot contain the value. When data is sorted or clustered on the filter column, each row group covers a narrow range, so most can be skipped. Compression does not affect skipping, and partitioning by a high-cardinality key creates a huge number of tiny folders.

title: Hundreds of files in every date partition
question: A Spark job runs df.repartition(200).write.partitionBy("event_date").parquet(path) over 90 days of data and produces about 200 small files in every event_date folder. What change produces few, larger files per date?
options: Call coalesce(1) before writing so a single task writes all the output
Repartition by event_date before writing so each date is in few tasks
Raise spark.sql.files.maxPartitionBytes so more data goes per file
Replace partitionBy with bucketBy(200) on the event_date column
explanation: partitionBy writes one file per task per partition value present in that task. After a random repartition(200), every task holds rows for almost every date, so each date folder gets about 200 files. Repartitioning by event_date (optionally with a few sub-partitions) puts each date's rows in few tasks. coalesce(1) creates a single-task bottleneck, and maxPartitionBytes affects reading, not writing.

title: Appending a DataFrame with a new column to Delta
question: A job appends a DataFrame to a Delta Lake table, but the DataFrame now has an extra column, discount_code, and the write fails with a schema mismatch error. The new column is intended. What should the job do?
options: Write with mode('overwrite') so the whole table takes the new schema
Drop the existing table and recreate it from the new DataFrame
Write the new column to a separate Parquet folder beside the table
Append with the mergeSchema option so the new column is added
explanation: Delta Lake enforces the table schema on write and rejects unexpected columns to protect data quality. When a new column is intentional, the mergeSchema option (or automatic schema merging) evolves the table by adding the column during the append. Overwriting or recreating the table destroys existing data, and a side folder breaks the table's consistency.

title: Testing a primary key column in dbt
question: In dbt, which built-in generic data tests together assert that a model's primary key column has no duplicate values and no missing values?
options: unique and not_null
relationships and unique
accepted_values and not_null
freshness and relationships
explanation: dbt ships four generic data tests: unique, not_null, accepted_values and relationships. Applying unique and not_null to a key column checks that it identifies each row. accepted_values limits a column to a list of values, relationships checks referential integrity against another model, and freshness is a source check rather than a data test.

title: Compatibility mode when producers upgrade first
question: A producer will start publishing records with a new schema version immediately, while some consumers keep running the old schema for weeks. Which minimal Schema Registry compatibility mode ensures those old consumers can still read the new data?
options: BACKWARD
FORWARD
NONE
BACKWARD_TRANSITIVE
explanation: FORWARD compatibility means data written with the new schema can be read by consumers using the previous schema, which is the requirement when producers upgrade before consumers. BACKWARD (and its transitive variant) guarantees the opposite direction, new readers reading old data, which fits upgrading consumers first. NONE performs no checks at all.

title: Renaming a column in a large Delta table
question: A 40 TB Delta Lake table has a column named cust_nm that must be renamed to customer_name. Rewriting all data files is too expensive. What enables a metadata-only rename?
options: Create a view that exposes cust_nm under the new name
Run ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN; Delta always renames in place
Enable column mapping mode 'name', then use RENAME COLUMN
Add customer_name with mergeSchema and copy values in place
explanation: By default Delta resolves columns by their physical names in the Parquet files, so a rename would require rewriting data. Enabling column mapping (delta.columnMapping.mode = 'name') decouples logical and physical names, allowing RENAME COLUMN and DROP COLUMN as metadata-only operations, at the cost of a table protocol upgrade. Adding and backfilling a new column rewrites the data, and a view only hides the problem.
